subject: iot
title: Unit 2 MCQs — IoT Sensors & Embedded Systems

items.q: What is the precise relationship between a sensor, a transducer, and an actuator?
options: They are three names for the same device
Every sensor and actuator is a transducer; a sensor measures (input), an actuator acts (output)
A transducer is a type of sensor that cannot be an actuator
An actuator senses while a sensor acts
items.explain: A transducer converts one energy form to another. A sensor is a transducer on the input/measurement side (physical → electrical); an actuator is one on the output side (electrical → physical action).

items.q: Sensors are often called the '___ of IoT' because they convert physical phenomena into measurable signals.
items.explain: Sensors are the eyes and ears of IoT — they perceive the physical world. (Actuators are the 'hands'; the processor is the 'brain'.)

items.q: Which group lists only ACTIVE sensors?
items.explain: Active sensors emit energy and measure the reflection: ultrasonic (sound), radar (radio), LiDAR (laser). Thermocouple, LDR, and PIR are passive — they detect existing natural energy.

items.q: A PIR (Passive Infrared) sensor detects people because it:
options: Emits an infrared beam and measures the reflection
Detects the infrared heat naturally radiated by a human body (emits nothing)
Uses a laser to map the room
items.explain: PIR is passive: it detects IR radiation emitted by warm bodies without emitting any energy itself. An active IR proximity sensor, by contrast, emits an IR beam.

items.q: A thermocouple inserted into an engine cylinder to read internal temperature is an example of a(n) ___ sensor.
items.explain: It penetrates/embeds into the measured system (invasive) and contacts it directly. An IR thermometer reading surface temperature from a distance would be non-invasive and no-contact.

items.q: On a dartboard analogy, darts tightly clustered together but far from the bullseye represent a sensor that is:
items.explain: Tight cluster = high precision (consistent); wrong spot = low accuracy (not close to true value). This is a systematic error that calibration can correct.

items.q: The smallest change in the measured quantity that a sensor can detect is its:
items.explain: Resolution is the smallest detectable change. Sensitivity is the output change per unit input (slope) — a different property.

items.q: A load cell outputs 0.05 V when no load is applied. This non-zero output at zero input is called:
items.explain: Offset (bias) is the baseline output when input is zero. Drift, by contrast, is a slow change over time. Offset is corrected during calibration (auto-zero).

items.q: A sensor's reading slowly creeps upward over weeks even though the true input is constant. This is:
items.explain: Drift is a slow change in output over time (ageing/temperature) for a fixed input — the reason sensors need periodic recalibration.

items.q: Response time is typically defined as the time for a sensor to reach what fraction of its final value after a step change?
items.explain: Response time is measured to a defined settling threshold, typically 90% or 95% of the final value after a step input.

items.q: Which metric, measured in hertz, is the range of input frequencies a sensor can track without distortion?
items.explain: Bandwidth (Hz) is the usable frequency range. Wide bandwidth is needed for vibration/audio sensing. Frequency response is the fuller amplitude/phase-vs-frequency curve.

items.q: Which set are all DYNAMIC performance metrics?
options: Response time, SNR, bandwidth, frequency response
items.explain: Dynamic metrics describe behaviour under change: response time, SNR, bandwidth, frequency response. Accuracy/precision/resolution/linearity/range/offset/drift are static.

items.q: For a solar-powered outdoor smart-parking sensor scaling to 100+ slots, which criterion is MOST decisive in the choice?
options: Maximum possible resolution regardless of cost
Ultra-low power + low cost + weatherproofing (binary presence is enough)
items.explain: The task only needs binary presence, so a low-cost, ultra-low-power, weatherproof IR/ultrasonic sensor fits the solar power, outdoor environment, and large-scale cost constraints.

items.q: What fundamentally distinguishes a sensor from an actuator?
options: A sensor is output (acts); an actuator is input (senses)
A sensor is input (senses data); an actuator is output (acts on the environment)
items.explain: A sensor detects changes (input). An actuator converts an electrical signal into a physical action (output) — e.g., a relay switching on a fan.

items.q: Which actuator type uses compressed air to produce motion?
items.explain: Pneumatic actuators use compressed air (e.g., pneumatic arms, air valves). Hydraulic uses pressurised fluid; thermal uses heat expansion; magnetic uses magnetic fields.

items.q: The key difference between open-loop and closed-loop actuator control is:
options: Open-loop is always digital; closed-loop is always analog
Closed-loop uses sensor feedback to self-correct; open-loop has no feedback
Open-loop is more reliable than closed-loop
items.explain: Closed-loop control uses sensor feedback to continuously adjust (e.g., blinds following a light sensor). Open-loop runs a fixed command with no feedback (e.g., a fixed-time sprinkler).

items.q: What makes a 'smart sensor' smart compared to a basic sensor?
options: It integrates signal conditioning, a microcontroller, and a comms interface to output a conditioned digital value (often self-calibrating)
It only outputs raw analog voltage
It requires an external ADC and manual calibration
items.explain: A smart sensor adds on-board processing (conditioning, ADC, MCU, comms) so it outputs a clean digital value, can self-calibrate and self-diagnose — pushing edge intelligence to the sensing element.

items.q: IEEE 1451's TEDS (Transducer Electronic Data Sheet) primarily enables:
options: Plug-and-play sensors that self-describe their identity and calibration data to any compatible host
items.explain: TEDS stores the sensor's identity, calibration, and characteristics in on-board memory, so a sensor can announce itself for true plug-and-play interoperability.

items.q: Which is NOT one of the defining capabilities of a smart object?
options: Sensing and actuation with embedded logic
Requiring a continuous human operator to function
items.explain: Smart objects are autonomous. Their defining capabilities are unique identity, sensing, processing, communication, and actuation+logic — they act without constant human control.

items.q: A vibration sensor on a machine transmitting at hundreds of Hz is classified as a ___ smart object by reporting frequency.
items.explain: High reporting frequency = rapid, frequent updates (e.g., machine vibration). A rust sensor sending monthly data is low-reporting. (Mobility is a separate axis: static vs mobile.)

items.q: MEMS stands for, and is fabricated using:
options: Multi-Element Memory Systems; assembled by hand
Macro-Electrical Mechanical Sensors; cast in metal
items.explain: MEMS = Micro-Electro-Mechanical Systems — micro/millimetre-scale mechanical+electrical elements built on silicon wafers via photolithography.

items.q: A smartphone's screen-rotation and a drone's stabilization rely respectively on MEMS:
items.explain: A MEMS accelerometer senses tilt/linear acceleration (screen rotation); a MEMS gyroscope senses angular rotation rate (drone stabilization). Together they form an IMU.

items.q: In an IMU, why are an accelerometer and gyroscope fused together?
options: They measure the same thing for redundancy only
Their flaws are complementary — the accelerometer is noisy but drift-free; the gyroscope is smooth but drifts — so fusing gives a smooth AND stable estimate
The gyroscope is accurate long-term and the accelerometer short-term
Neither is useful alone or together
items.explain: Accelerometer: noisy but no long-term drift. Gyroscope: smooth short-term but accumulates drift. Fusion (complementary/Kalman filter) trusts each where it's strong, yielding orientation that's both smooth and stable.

items.q: Using three temperature sensors and voting out a faulty one is which kind of sensor fusion?
items.explain: Competitive/redundant fusion uses multiple sensors measuring the SAME quantity for fault tolerance and noise reduction. Complementary covers different aspects; cooperative derives new info (e.g., stereo depth).

items.q: Which algorithm is the classic optimal estimator used to fuse noisy sensor data with a predict–correct cycle?
items.explain: The Kalman filter optimally fuses noisy measurements via predict-then-correct, weighting sensors by trust. The Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) handles non-linear systems (drones, GPS+IMU).

items.q: A two-point calibration (e.g., ice at 0°C and boiling water at 100°C) primarily corrects:
items.explain: One point fixes offset; two points fix both offset and gain (the line y = gain·x + offset). Multi-point calibration also corrects non-linearity.

items.q: Why is self-calibration especially valuable in IoT?
options: Sensors are deployed at scale, unattended for years, where drift accumulates and manual recalibration is impractical
It removes the need for any sensors
It only matters for laboratory equipment
items.explain: Large, unattended, long-lived field deployments can't be hand-recalibrated. Self-calibration (auto-zero, internal references, temperature compensation) keeps data trustworthy without truck-rolls.

items.q: In a Wireless Sensor Network, the base station that collects data from all nodes is also called the:
items.explain: The base station is the sink or gateway. Each node (sensor + MCU + radio + battery) forwards its data there, typically in a unidirectional flow.

items.q: Which best captures the WSN-vs-IoT relationship?
options: A WSN is a subset of IoT focused on sensing/forwarding (often unidirectional); IoT is the full ecosystem with processing, actuation, analytics, and bidirectional control
IoT is a subset of WSN
items.explain: A WSN handles sensing and basic data transmission (usually sensor → gateway → app). IoT is the broader, bidirectional ecosystem adding edge intelligence, actuation, analytics, and cloud integration.

items.q: Energy-harvesting sensors are pivotal to 'Green IoT' because they:
options: Scavenge ambient energy (light, vibration, heat) so they need no battery — enabling sustainable, maintenance-free deployment of billions of nodes
Are physically larger and easier to service
items.explain: By harvesting ambient energy, these sensors run without batteries, removing IoT's biggest bottleneck (power) and making massive, unattended, sustainable deployments feasible.

items.q: How does a microcontroller (MCU) differ from a microprocessor?
options: An MCU is only the CPU core with no memory
An MCU integrates CPU + memory (flash/RAM) + peripherals on one chip; a microprocessor is just the core needing external support
A microprocessor is always cheaper and smaller
items.explain: A microcontroller is a complete computer-on-a-chip (CPU + flash + SRAM + GPIO/timers/ADC/comms), ideal for embedded/IoT. A microprocessor is just the processing core requiring external RAM, storage, and peripherals.

items.q: Embedded systems are characterised by all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Designed for a specific task and often real-time
Limited memory and compute, often no OS (or an RTOS)
Abundant RAM and a full desktop operating system by default
items.explain: Embedded systems are resource-constrained and usually bare-metal or RTOS-based — not running a full desktop OS with abundant RAM.

items.q: STM32 microcontrollers are based on which processor architecture?
items.explain: STM32 (STMicroelectronics) is a family of 32-bit ARM Cortex-M microcontrollers, available in series like F1 (general), L (low-power), and F4 (high-performance).

items.q: Which STM32 on-chip peripheral is used to read an analog sensor voltage?
items.explain: The ADC (Analog-to-Digital Converter) converts an analog sensor voltage into a digital value. GPIO handles digital I/O; UART is serial comms; flash stores firmware.

items.q: In the STM32 'blink' example, what do HAL_GPIO_TogglePin() and HAL_Delay() represent?
options: HAL (Hardware Abstraction Layer) calls that hide raw register writes behind readable functions
items.explain: HAL functions abstract the underlying register manipulation; combined with CubeMX-generated setup code, they let you focus on logic in the super-loop.

items.q: UART on an STM32 is commonly used to:
options: Provide serial debug output and communicate with modules like GPS, Bluetooth, or a Wi-Fi modem
items.explain: UART (serial) is used for debug consoles and to talk to external modules (GPS, BT, modems) — often the bridge that connects a standalone MCU to the network.
